approach: 1. Method Optimization: Evaluated GC/MS conditions using a high-polarity PEG column without derivatization. Compared four organic solvents (MTBE, diethyl ether, chloroform, n-hexane) for LLE efficiency and background noise. Selected MTBE based on high recovery and low interference. Tested surrogate matrices (charcoal-stripped plasma, BSA solution, distilled water) by comparing spike recovery against authentic biological matrices. 2. Validation: Validated the method according to bioanalytical guidelines, assessing linearity (calibration curves), precision (inter-day RSD), parallelism (slope comparison between water and biological matrices), recovery (spiked vs. unspiked), and matrix effect. 3. Application: Quantified SCFAs in 10 human plasma, 20 serum, 10 feces, and 6 mouse cecum tissue samples to demonstrate practical applicability.

contribution_and_limits.contribution: Provides a simplified, derivatization-free GC/MS protocol for SCFA quantification that reduces instrument contamination and analysis time.
contribution_and_limits.limits: The surrogate matrix approach relies on the assumption that water mimics the extraction behavior of complex biological matrices; this may not hold for all sample types or analytes outside the tested range.

contribution_and_limits.contribution: Validates the use of distilled water as a cost-effective and accessible surrogate matrix for SCFA calibration across multiple biological fluids and tissues.
contribution_and_limits.limits: Validation was performed on a limited number of sample origins (e.g., six different origins per matrix type for matrix effect testing); broader population variability is not assessed.

contribution_and_limits.contribution: Offers specific mass spectrometry parameters (SIM ions, retention times) for acetic, propionic, butyric, and valeric acids, facilitating method implementation.
contribution_and_limits.limits: The method focuses only on four common SCFAs; other microbial metabolites are not addressed.

key_findings.finding: Diethyl ether showed the highest extraction recovery but produced significant background noise for acetic acid due to oxidation. Methyl tert-butyl ether (MTBE) was selected as it provided good recovery with minimal interference.

Charcoal-stripped plasma contained residual SCFAs and was discarded. BSA solution showed low recovery. Distilled water exhibited extraction recovery similar to that in plasma, serum, feces, and cecum tissue, making it a feasible surrogate matrix.

The method showed good linearity (R² > 0.99), inter-day precision (RSD < 10%), and recovery (94.89–109.32%). Matrix effects were within 97.18–108.37%. Parallelism slopes between water and biological matrices ranged from 0.97 to 1.02, with relative errors < 10%.

Acetic acid was the dominant SCFA in all sample types. In human serum, the ratio of acetic:propionic:butyric acid was approximately 92:7:1. In human feces, the ratio was 53:26:21. Some butyric and valeric acid levels in plasma were below the limit of quantification.

problem_or_question: Accurate quantification of SCFAs is critical for understanding gut microbiome-host interactions in diseases like IBD, obesity, and diabetes. Existing methods often require time-consuming precolumn derivatization or suffer from high background noise and GC/MS contamination due to direct aqueous injection or unsuitable solvents. Additionally, the lack of metabolite-free biological matrices complicates the preparation of calibration standards, leading to potential matrix effects.
research_scope: Human plasma, serum, feces, and mouse cecum tissue; Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs: acetic, propionic, butyric, valeric acids); Gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC/MS).
work_summary: This study developed and validated an improved GC/MS method for the simultaneous quantification of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) in diverse biological samples. The authors optimized a liquid-liquid extraction (LLE) procedure using methyl tert-butyl ether (MTBE) to extract SCFAs from acidified samples without derivatization, thereby reducing contamination of the GC/MS system. A key innovation was the selection of distilled water as a surrogate matrix for calibration, which demonstrated parallelism and similar extraction recovery to complex biological matrices like plasma, serum, feces, and cecum tissue. The method was validated for linearity, precision, recovery, and matrix effect, and successfully applied to quantify SCFAs in small cohorts of human and mouse samples.
